common_name: Decadence Deluxe Blue Bubbly Baptisia (Tall Lavender-Blue False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Blue Bubbly is a larger-growing Decadence Deluxe selection bred for extra-long flower spikes.

directions: Blue Bubbly carries dense, airy spikes of lavender-blue, pea-like flowers up to 16 inches long that rise well above the blue-green foliage in a vase-shaped, upright mound, one of the largest-flowering selections in the Decadence Deluxe line. It blooms a little later and a little longer than most compact Baptisia cultivars, giving way afterward to dark, rattling seedpods that carry the display into fall and winter. Give it a permanent spot in well-drained, average soil in full sun, since its deep taproot makes established plants very difficult to move successfully. Once settled it is extremely drought-tolerant, deer-resistant, and essentially maintenance-free, needing only an occasional late-winter cutback rather than division.

common_name: Decadence Deluxe Pink Lemonade Baptisia (Yellow-to-Raspberry Color-Changing False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Pink Lemonade's flower spikes change color noticeably as they age.

directions: Pink Lemonade opens with soft butter-yellow flowers on tall spikes that gradually age to a dusty raspberry-purple, so a single plant often shows both colors at once partway through its late-spring-to-early-summer bloom, an unusual two-tone effect within the Decadence Deluxe line. The sturdy, upright, densely branched habit needs no staking, and the spent flower spikes ripen into dark, ornamental seedpods that persist well into fall. Plant it in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun and pick a permanent location, since mature Baptisia resent root disturbance from their deep taproot. It is drought-tolerant and pest-resistant once established, drawing bees heavily during its bloom window and needing little more than an optional late-winter tidy-up.

common_name: Decadence Deluxe Periwinkle Popsicle Baptisia (Late-Blooming Deep Periwinkle False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Periwinkle Popsicle blooms slightly later than most Baptisia, extending the false-indigo season.

directions: Periwinkle Popsicle bears saturated, deep periwinkle-blue flower spikes on a tall, vase-shaped plant, standing out among Decadence Deluxe siblings for opening slightly later in the season and so stretching the false-indigo bloom window into a later slot in the perennial border. Its dark seedpods add textural interest through fall and winter after the flowers fade. Site it in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade, choosing a permanent spot since its deep taproot makes established plants poor candidates for moving or dividing. Like the rest of the genus it is long-lived, drought-tolerant once rooted in, and a larval host for several native butterflies, requiring little care beyond an optional late-winter cutback.

common_name: Decadence Dark Chocolate Baptisia (Long-Spiked Charcoal-Purple False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Dark Chocolate is an improved sport of the older Dutch Chocolate selection with notably longer flower spikes.

directions: Dark Chocolate produces nearly black, charcoal-purple pea-like flowers packed onto spikes that can stretch to over two feet, noticeably longer than those of the similarly colored Dutch Chocolate that preceded it in the Decadence line, on a compact, densely branched, upright mound. The unusually dark bloom color reads almost black in low light and stands out sharply against the blue-green foliage from late spring into early summer. Grow it in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since the deep taproot makes mature plants intolerant of moving or dividing. It is deer-resistant, drought-tolerant once established, and popular with butterflies and cut-flower gardeners for its dramatic spike form.

common_name: Gallo Peach Blanket Flower (Dwarf Apricot-Peach Gaillardia)

planting.note: Set out plugs or container plants around the last frost into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Gallo Peach is a patented, seed-propagated dwarf selection bred to stay compact without staking.

directions: Gallo Peach is one of the smallest blanket flower selections widely grown, forming a tight, rounded mound only about 10 to 12 inches tall that carries soft apricot-peach ray flowers with a yellow-tipped edge over a long summer-into-fall bloom season. Its dwarf, well-branched habit fits neatly along a border edge or in a container where taller Gaillardia would flop, and it needs no deadheading to keep flowering steadily. Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun, since like all Gaillardia it declines quickly in heavy, wet ground. It draws bees and butterflies reliably through its bloom window and tolerates heat and drought with ease once established.

common_name: Gallo Red Blanket Flower (Dwarf Solid Red-Orange Gaillardia)

planting.note: Set out plugs or container plants around the last frost into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Gallo Red is a companion selection to Gallo Peach in the same dwarf, seed-propagated series.

directions: Gallo Red forms the same tight, dwarf mound as its Gallo-series relatives but carries rich red-orange ray petals surrounding a rust-colored central disc, giving it a warmer, more solid-toned look than the bicolor Gallo Peach. It flowers non-stop from early summer through fall on a compact plant that never needs staking or pinching, making it a dependable choice for the front of a hot, sunny border. Plant in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun, since excess moisture around the crown is the most common cause of decline in any Gaillardia. Once established it tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil with ease, and its long bloom season keeps bees and butterflies visiting steadily.

common_name: Lunar Harvest Moon Blanket Flower (Dwarf Yellow-and-Red Gaillardia)

planting.note: Set out container plants around the last frost into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Harvest Moon belongs to the extra-dwarf Lunar series bred for tidy container and edging use.

directions: Harvest Moon is among the most diminutive blanket flowers grown, part of the Lunar series that tops out around 8 to 10 inches, with warm yellow ray petals shading to red toward the central disc for a two-toned, sunburst look. It blooms continuously from early summer well into fall on a dense, mounding plant that suits a container, rock garden edge, or the front of a sunny bed where larger Gaillardia would overwhelm the space. Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun, since the compact Lunar series is just as intolerant of wet feet as full-sized blanket flowers. It is heat- and drought-tolerant once rooted in and draws bees and butterflies steadily through its long bloom run.
sources: University of Georgia Trial Gardens evaluation

common_name: Sundance Bicolor Blanket Flower (Double Mahogany-and-Yellow Firewheel)

planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants after the last frost into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Sundance Bicolor is grown as a warm-season annual and reseeds readily where conditions suit it.

directions: Sundance Bicolor was an All-America Selections bedding-plant winner recognized for producing the first reliably double, fully globe-shaped blanket flowers in a consistent mahogany-red-and-yellow bicolor pattern, a marked departure from the flat, single blooms typical of wild firewheel. It flowers from within weeks of germination straight through the heat of summer into fall on a spreading, well-branched plant suited equally to open beds, containers, or hanging baskets. Direct sow or transplant into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun after frost danger passes, since like all Gaillardia it dislikes rich, moisture-retentive ground. Deadheading is optional, as it blooms prolifically regardless, and it self-sows freely in warm climates where its parent species is native.
